# I. Introduction {background-color="#15797A"} ## I. Introduction {auto-animate="true"} ### Supervised Learning Setting :::{style="font-size: 80%"} > **Objective:** Predicting target $y$ using input $x$. - If $y$ is continuous, the problem is called `Regression`. - If $y$ is discrete/categorical, it's called `Classification`. > **Criteria** - Quality of a prediction $\hat{y}$ is measured by the loss: $\ell(\hat{y},y)$. - Quality of a model $\hat{f}$ is measured by the risk: $${\cal R}(\hat{f})=\mathbb{E}_{X,Y}[\ell(Y, \hat{f}(X))].$$ ::: ## I. Introduction {auto-animate="true"} ### Supervised Learning Setting :::{style="font-size: 80%"} - **Parametric models** assume a specific form that depends on a fixed number of parameters. Example: - Linear model: $\hat{f}_{\color{blue}{\beta}}(\text{x})=\color{blue}{\beta_0}+\sum_{j=1}^d\color{blue}{\beta_j}x_j$ with $\color{blue}{\beta_0},\dots,\color{blue}{\beta_d}\in\mathbb{R}.$ - Polynomial model: $\hat{f}_{\color{blue}{\beta}}(\text{x})=\color{blue}{\beta_0}+\sum_{p=0}^m\sum_{k=1}^d\sum_{j\leq k}\color{blue}{\beta_{jkp}}x_j^{p}x_k^{m-p}$ with $\color{blue}{\beta_0},\color{blue}{\beta_{jkp}}\in\mathbb{R},\forall j,k,p.$ - $2$-layer Neural Networks: $\hat{f}(\text{x})=\sigma_2\left(\color{blue}{W_2}\sigma_1(\color{blue}{W_1}x+\color{blue}{b_1})+\color{blue}{b_2}\right).$ - Building a model is searching for $\color{blue}{\beta^*}$ minimizing the risk, i.e., $${\cal R}(\hat{f}_{\color{blue}{\beta^*}})=\inf_{\color{blue}{\beta}}\Big[\underbrace{{\cal R}(\hat{f}_{\color{blue}{\beta}})}_{\text{Goodness of fit}} + \underbrace{\color{gray}{\Omega(\color{blue}{\beta})}}_{\text{Flexibility}}\Big]$$ ::: ## I. Introduction {auto-animate="true"} ### Supervised Learning Setting :::{style="font-size: 80%"} - **Nonparametric models** rely directly on the target $y$ without assuming any form of input-output relationship. :::{.columns} :::{.column width="65%" style="font-size: 90%"} - General weighted average form: $$\hat{f}(\text{x})=\sum_{i=1}^ny_i\color{blue}{W_{n,i}(\text{x})}.$$ - Interpretation: - The prediction of $\text{x}$ is determined by averaging values of targets $y_i$'s. - Targets $y_i$ that their input $\text{x}_i$ is **similar** to $\text{x}$ are more important and carry heavier weight $\color{blue}{W_{n,i}(\text{x})}$ in the average. ::: :::{.column width="35%"} ![](./img/neighbors.png){width="400px" fig-align="center"} :::{.fragment style="font-size: 85%"} 🤔 Why does it work? ::: :::{.fragment style="font-size: 85%"} 🗝️ Because it estimates $\color{red}{\eta(x)=\mathbb{E}(Y|X=x)}$. ::: :::{.fragment style="font-size: 85%"} 🤔 But what's this $\color{red}{\eta(x)}$? ::: ::: ::: ::: # II. Theoretical Motivation {background-color="#15797A"} ## II. Theoretical Motivation {auto-animate="true"} ### 1. Regression theory: $L_2$/MSE minimizer :::{style="font-size:80%" .incremental} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="80%"} - $\color{blue}{\text{Mean Squared Error}}$ of any model $\hat{f}$ is defined by: $$\color{blue}{\text{MSE}}(\hat{f})=\mathbb{E}[(\hat{f}(X)-Y)^2].$$ - If $\text{x}$ be an input and $\color{red}{\eta(\text{x})=\mathbb{E}(Y|X=\text{x})}$ then $\forall\hat{f}$: $$\begin{align*} \color{blue}{\text{MSE}}(\hat{f})&=\mathbb{E}[(\hat{f}(X)-\color{red}{\eta}(X))^2]+\mathbb{E}[(\color{red}{\eta}(X)-Y)^2] \end{align*}$$ - This implies that $\color{red}{\eta}$ is the **minimizer** of $\color{blue}{\text{MSE}}$ criterion, i.e., $$\color{blue}{\text{MSE}}(\color{red}{\eta})=\inf_{\hat{f}}\color{blue}{\text{MSE}}(\hat{f})=\mathbb{E}[(\color{red}{\eta}(X)-Y)^2].$$ - $\color{red}{\eta}$ is called **Regression Function/$L_2$ Bayesian Estimator.** ::: :::{.column width="20%" .fragment} [![](./img/pattern_rec.png){width="120px"}](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/b97848){target="_blank"}
[![](./img/a_dist_free.png){width="120px"}](https://www.szit.bme.hu/~gyorfi/pbook.pdf){target="_blank"}
[![](./img/ELSL.jpg){width="120px"}](https://www.stat.ntu.edu.tw/download/教學文件/bigdata/The%20Elements%20of%20Statistical%20Learning.pdf){target="_blank"} ::: ::: ::: ## II. Theoretical Motivation {auto-animate="true"} ### 1. Regression theory: $L_2$/MSE minimizer - $\color{red}{\eta}$ is called **Regression Function/$L_2$ Bayesian Estimator.** :::{.incremental} - $\color{red}{\eta(\text{x})=\mathbb{E}(Y|X=\text{x})}$ **is the average of $y$ for inputs that are similar to the query point** $\text{x}$. In discrete case: $$\begin{align*}\color{red}{\eta}(\text{x})&=\mathbb{E}(Y|X=\text{x})=\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}y_i\color{blue}{\mathbb{P}(Y=y_i|X=\text{x})} \end{align*}$$ - Recall that nonparam. models: $\hat{f}(\text{x})=\sum_{i=1}^ny_i\color{blue}{W_{n,i}(\text{x})}.$ ::: ## II. Theoretical Motivation {auto-animate="true"} ### 1. Regression theory: $L_2$/MSE minimizer :::{.columns style="font-size: 80%"} :::{.column width="50%"} - **Nonparametric models:** $$\hat{f}(\text{x})=\sum_{i=1}^ny_i\color{blue}{W_{n,i}(\text{x})}.$$ ::: :::{.column width="50%"} - **Regression function:** $$\color{red}{\eta}(\text{x})=\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}y_i\color{blue}{\mathbb{P}(Y=y_i|X=\text{x})}.$$ ::: :::{.incremental style="font-size:90%"} - [Q1:]{.light-red} Why don't we compute $\color{blue}{\mathbb{P}(Y=y_i|X=\text{x})}$ directly? - [A1:]{.green} We don't know the distribution of $Y|X$. - Weights $\color{blue}{W_{n,i}(\text{x})}$ plays a role as an estimate of $\color{blue}{\mathbb{P}(Y=y_i|X=\text{x})}$. - Different choices of weights lead to different nonparametric models. - Weights $\color{blue}{W_{n,i}(\text{x})}$ are often defined according to how "close" $\text{x}_i$ to $\text{x}$. - "Closeness" is often described by "metrics, neighborhoods or topological structures"... ::: ::: ## II. Theoretical Motivation {auto-animate="true"} ### 2. Example: Missing Value Imputation :::{style="font-size: 80%"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} ```{python} #| echo: true #| code-fold: true #| fig-align: "center" from skimage import data import matplotlib.pyplot as plt image = data.astronaut() import numpy as np from sklearn.impute import KNNImputer n_miss = 100 np.random.seed(42) missing_id = np.random.choice(512, size=(n_miss,2)) image_nan = image.copy() for i in range(n_miss): image_nan[(missing_id[i,0]-2):(missing_id[i,0]+2),(missing_id[i,1]-2):(missing_id[i,1]+2),:] = 0 plt.figure(figsize=(4,4)) plt.imshow(image_nan) plt.axis('off') plt.show() ``` ::: :::{.column width="50%" .fragment} ```{python} #| echo: true #| code-fold: true #| fig-align: "center" for i in range(n_miss): for ch in range(3): temp = image_nan[(missing_id[i,0]-5):(missing_id[i,0]+5), (missing_id[i,1]-5):(missing_id[i,1]+5), ch] image_nan[(missing_id[i,0]-2):(missing_id[i,0]+2),(missing_id[i,1]-2):(missing_id[i,1]+2),ch] = temp[temp> 0].mean() plt.figure(figsize=(4,4)) plt.imshow(image_nan) plt.axis('off') plt.show() ``` ::: :::{.fragment style="font-size:90%" .incremental} - Missing pixels $=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^Np_k$ where $p_k$ are neighboring non-missing pixels. - [Q2:]{.light-red} What are the weights $\color{blue}{W_{n,i}(\text{x})}$ in this case? ::: ::: ::: ## II. Theoretical Motivation {auto-animate="true"} ### 3. Decision theory for classification :::{style="font-size: 65%"} - In classification, **misclassification loss**: $\ell(\hat{f}(x),y)=\mathbb{1}_{\{\hat{f}(x)\neq y\}}=\begin{cases}1,\text{ if }\hat{f}(x)\neq y\\0,\text{ if }\hat{f}(x)=y\end{cases}$. - The **misclassification risk** is given by: $${\cal R}_c(\hat{f})=\mathbb{E}[\ell(\hat{f}(X),Y)]=\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{1}_{\{\hat{f}(X)\neq Y\}}]=\mathbb{P}(\hat{f}(X)\neq Y).$$ - This is equivalent to classification problems that maximize **accuracy** score because $$\text{Accuracy}=1-\mathbb{P}(\hat{f}(X)\neq Y)=\mathbb{P}(\hat{f}(X)=Y).$$ ::: :::{.sbr} ::: :::{.callout-tip icon=false} ### Lemma [[Ch 2, Hastie et al. (2008)](https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~fdiebold/NoHesitations/BookAdvanced.pdf){target="_blank"} & [Sec 1.4, Kyörfi et al. (2002)](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/b97848)] In **balanced** $M$-class classification, $$\text{If } g^*(x)=\arg\max_{1\leq k\leq M}\mathbb{P}(Y=k|X=x)\text{ then }{\cal R}_c(g^*)=\inf_{\hat{f}}{\cal R}_c(\hat{f}).$$ ::: ## II. Theoretical Motivation {auto-animate="true"} ### Summary :::{style="font-size: 80%" .incremental} - In regression with [MSE]{.light-blue}, $\color{red}{\eta(\text{x})=\mathbb{E}(Y|X=\text{x})}$ is the **best regressor**. - We cannot compute it, but we can estimate it. - **Parametric models** assume that $\color{red}{\eta}$ takes some forms (linear, polynomial...). - **Nonparametric models** attempt to estimate $\color{red}{\eta}$ using weighted average form: $\hat{f}(\text{x})=\sum_{i=1}^ny_i\color{blue}{W_{n,i}(x)}$. - In balanced $M$-class classification with **Accuracy** score, $g^*(\text{x})=\arg\max_{1\leq k\leq M}\color{blue}{\mathbb{P}(Y=k|X=\text{x})}$ is the **best classifier**. - We will now look at **three different models** that attempt to estimate regression function $\color{red}{\eta}$ using different form of weights $\color{blue}{W_{n,i}(\text{x})}$. ::: # III. $K$-Nearest Neighbors ($K$-NN) {background-color="#15797A"} ## III. $K$-Nearest Neighbors ($K$-NN) {auto-animate="true"} ### 1. Setting :::{style="font-size: 70%"} - Given `iid` observations: $\{(\text{x}_1,y_1),\dots, (\text{x}_n,y_n)\}\subset \mathbb{R}^d\times{\cal Y}$. - If $D$ is a distance on $\mathbb{R}^d$ (e.g. Euclidean distance), the **$k$-th nearest neighbor** $\color{red}{\text{x}_{(k)}}$ of $\text{x}\in\mathbb{R}^d$ is defined by - $D(\text{x},\text{x}_{(1)})\leq D(\text{x},\text{x}_{(2)})\leq\dots\leq D(\text{x},\color{red}{\text{x}_{(k)}})\leq \dots\leq D(\text{x},\text{x}_{(n)})$. - Let $y_{(1)},\dots,y_{(n)}$ be the target of $\text{x}_{(1)},\dots,\text{x}_{(n)}$ respectively. - If $K\geq 1$, then $K$-NN predicts the target of an input $\text{x}$ by :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%" style="font-size:90%"} - **Regression:** $$\begin{align*}\hat{y}&=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^Ky_{(k)}\qquad\quad \color{gray}{(\color{blue}{W_{n,i}(\text{x})}=?)}\\ &=\text{Average $y_{(k)}$ among the $K$ neighbors}.\end{align*}$$ ::: :::{.column width="50%" style="font-size:90%"} - **Classification:** $$\begin{align*}\hat{y}&=\arg\max_{1\leq m\leq M}\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^K\mathbb{1}_{\{y^{(k)}=m\}}\\ &=\text{Majority class among the $K$ neighbors.}\end{align*}$$ ::: ::: ::: ## III. $K$-Nearest Neighbors ($K$-NN) {auto-animate="true"} ### 2. Curse of dimensionality :::{style="font-size:75%"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="60%" style="font-size: 80%" .incremental} - **[Curse of dimensionality]{.light-red}** refers to various challenges and phenomena that arise when working with high-dimensional data. - The main challenge for $K$-NN is that **[distances]{.light-blue}** or **[closeness]{.light-blue}** lose its meaning in high-dimensional spaces. - In this scenario, data points tend to be equally distant from one another. - Example: Simulate $\text{x}_1,\dots,\text{x}_n\sim{\cal U}[-5,5]^d$ with $d=1,10,100,500,1000, 5000, 10000, 50000$. - For each dimension $d$, we compute: $$r(d)=\frac{\max_{i\neq j}D(\text{x}_i,\text{x}_j)}{\min_{i\neq j}D(\text{x}_i,\text{x}_j)}.$$ - Obtain the following graph 👉 ::: :::{.column width="40%" .fragment} ```{python} #| echo: true #| code-fold: true N = 10 Ds = np.zeros(shape=(N*(N-1)//2, 8)) j = 0 for d in [1,10,100, 500, 1000, 5000, 10000, 50000]: Xd = np.random.uniform(-5,5,size=(N,d)) i = 0 for s in range(1, N): for k in range(s): Ds[i,j] = np.linalg.norm(Xd[s,:] - Xd[k,:]) i += 1 j += 1 import plotly.express as px df_dist = pd.DataFrame({'Ratio': np.round(Ds.max(axis=0)/Ds.min(axis=0), 2), 'Dim': ['1','10','100', '500', '1000', '5000', '10000', '50000']}) fig4 = px.line(df_dist, x='Dim', y="Ratio", text="Ratio") fig4.update_layout( width=400, height=450, title="Max-min distance ratio at various dimension") fig4.update_xaxes(title='Dimension') fig4.update_yaxes(title='Max-Min Distance Ratio') fig4.update_traces(textposition="top right") fig4.show() ``` ::: ::: ::: ## III. $K$-Nearest Neighbors ($K$-NN) {auto-animate="true" .scrollable} ### Summary :::{style="font-size: 70%"} - $K$-NN is a nonparametric model with weights: $\color{blue}{W_{n,i}(\text{x})=\frac{\mathbb{1}_{\{\text{x}_i\in{\cal N}_{\text{x}}\}}}{K}}$, where ${\cal N}_{\text{x}}=\{\text{x}_{(1)},\dots,\text{x}_{(K)}\}$ the set of the first $K$-nearest neighbors of $\text{x}$. ::: :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%" style="font-size: 70%"} - Less parameter to tune. ::: ::: :::{.column width="50%"} ::: {.callout-caution icon=false} ### Cons - **Computationally Intensive:** Can be computationally expensive, often require memory and processing power. - **Overfitting:** Due to its flexibility, it might overfit the data without careful fine-tuning. - **Interpretability:** Mostly not interpretable except for decision trees. - **Key Parameter Tuning:** It requires proper key parameter tuning. ::: ::: ::: :::{.center} ## 🥳 It's party time 🥂 {background-image="./img/end_page.jpg" background-opacity="0.3"}

Introduction {auto-animate="true"} ### Supervised Learning Setting :::{style="font-size: 80%"} - **Parametric models** assume a specific form that depends on a fixed number of parameters. Introduction {auto-animate="true"} ### Supervised Learning Setting :::{style="font-size: 80%"} - **Nonparametric models** rely directly on the target $y$ without assuming any form of input-output relationship. :::{.columns} :::{.column width="65%" style="font-size: 90%"} - General weighted average form: $$\hat{f}(\text{x})=\sum_{i=1}^ny_i\color{blue}{W_{n,i}(\text{x})}.$$ - Interpretation: - The prediction of $\text{x}$ is determined by averaging values of targets $y_i$'s. - Targets $y_i$ that their input $\text{x}_i$ is **similar** to $\text{x}$ are more important and carry heavier weight $\color{blue}{W_{n,i}(\text{x})}$ in the average. ::: :::{.column width="35%"} ![](./img/neighbors.png){width="400px" fig-align="center"} :::{.fragment style="font-size: 85%"} 🤔 Why does it work? ::: :::{.fragment style="font-size: 85%"} 🗝️ Because it estimates $\color{red}{\eta(x)=\mathbb{E}(Y|X=x)}$. ::: :::{.fragment style="font-size: 85%"} 🤔 But what's this $\color{red}{\eta(x)}$? ::: ::: ::: ::: # II. Decision theory for classification :::{style="font-size: 65%"} - In classification, **misclassification loss**: $\ell(\hat{f}(x),y)=\mathbb{1}_{\{\hat{f}(x)\neq y\}}=\begin{cases}1,\text{ if }\hat{f}(x)\neq y\\0,\text{ if }\hat{f}(x)=y\end{cases}$. - The **misclassification risk** is given by: $${\cal R}_c(\hat{f})=\mathbb{E}[\ell(\hat{f}(X),Y)]=\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{1}_{\{\hat{f}(X)\neq Y\}}]=\mathbb{P}(\hat{f}(X)\neq Y).$$ - This is equivalent to classification problems that maximize **accuracy** score because $$\text{Accuracy}=1-\mathbb{P}(\hat{f}(X)\neq Y)=\mathbb{P}(\hat{f}(X)=Y).$$ ::: :::{.sbr} ::: :::{.callout-tip icon=false} ### Lemma [[Ch 2, Hastie et al. (2002)](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/b97848)] In **balanced** $M$-class classification, $$\text{If } g^*(x)=\arg\max_{1\leq k\leq M}\mathbb{P}(Y=k|X=x)\text{ then }{\cal R}_c(g^*)=\inf_{\hat{f}}{\cal R}_c(\hat{f}).$$ ::: ## II. Kernel Smoothing Methods ### Summary :::{style='font-size:80%'} - Kernel smoother is a nonparametric model that assigns weight to each points using some kernel function $K$, i.e., $$W_{n,i}(\text{x})=\frac{K_h(\|\text{x}_i-\text{x}\|)}{\sum_{j=1}^nK_h(\|\text{x}_j-\text{x}\|)}.$$ - Training a Kernel Smoother is equivalent to tuning the smoothing parameter $h>0$ using, for example, cross validation error. - Preprocessing is essential: scaling, encoding, transformation,... - Just like in $K$-NN, it might not work well in high-dimensional case but can be improved using the same methods. ::: ## Nonparametric Methods (Summary) :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} ::: {.callout-tip icon=false} ### Pros - **Flexibility:** Do not assume specific form of model. - **No Distribution Assumptions:** Do not require assumptions about the data distribution. - **Performance on Large Datasets:** Decision Trees can handle high dimensional and large datasets. - **Model Complexity:** Its complexity grows with data complexity. Less parameter to tune. ::: ::: :::{.column width="50%"} ::: {.callout-caution icon=false} ### Cons - **Computationally Intensive:** Can be computationally expensive, often require memory and processing power. - **Overfitting:** Due to its flexibility, it might overfit the data without careful fine-tuning. - **Interpretability:** Mostly not interpretable except for decision trees. - **Key Parameter Tuning:** It requires proper key parameter tuning. ::: ::: ::: :::{.center} ## 🥳 It's party time 🥂 {background-image="./img/end_page.jpg" background-opacity="0.3"}
